analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements between employers that block each other from hiring workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Booker with one cosponsor, never left the Senate labor committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2021 with no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for companies — including fast-food chains and their franchisees — to sign agreements promising not to hire or recruit each other's workers. These "no-poach" deals limit where an employee can take a better job, which keeps wages down. The bill would let workers sue for damages and let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the ban, and it would require franchisors to strike any existing no-poach clauses from their franchise contracts within six months.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people, especially the millions employed at franchise chains like fast-food restaurants, where corporate parent and franchisee agreements not to hire each other's staff restrict workers' ability to move to a better-paying job across the street. The bill would give them the right to sue for actual and punitive damages plus attorney's fees if an employer signs, enforces, or threatens to enforce such an agreement.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for any entity to enter into a restrictive employment agreement — any deal between two or more employers that limits one from hiring, soliciting, or employing another's employees or former employees — or to enforce or threaten to enforce one.
It requires any franchisor whose franchise agreement already contains a no-poach clause to remove it within six months of enactment, wiping out existing agreements across the franchise economy.
It creates a private right of action: an affected individual can sue for actual damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees, and can file in any federal district court.
It gives the Federal Trade Commission authority to enforce the ban with the same powers it has under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

analysis.who_pays: Franchisors and large employers that use no-poach clauses — the franchise industry most of all. They would have to rewrite franchise contracts, face lawsuits from workers, and lose a tool that holds down labor costs by keeping employees from switching jobs. Small franchisees could also face litigation risk as parties to the affected agreements.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action with punitive damages and fee-shifting could generate substantial litigation, and small franchise owners who signed standard-form franchise contracts would be parties to agreements now carrying lawsuit exposure through no choice of their own.

Defenders of some contracts argue that agreements protecting training investments or brand standards serve a business purpose; the bill bans the entire category between employers rather than applying a case-by-case test of whether a restriction is reasonable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and direct: economists and antitrust enforcers have identified franchise no-poach agreements as a widespread practice that suppresses worker mobility and wages, and banning them targets the harm at its source. The main cost is litigation exposure that would fall partly on small franchisees who did not draft the agreements, and the bill's blanket ban leaves no room for individually justified restrictions. On balance the gains to workers outweigh the costs, and existing antitrust law already treats some of these agreements as unlawful.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the End Employer Collusion Act in the Senate on July 23, 2019, with Senator Elizabeth Warren as cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken — no hearings, no markup, no committee or floor vote appear in the bill's action history through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.
Only one senator ever cosponsored the bill, so it never built the support needed to move through committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Franchisors and large chain employers that use no-poach clauses keep them in place, and their workers remain subject to agreements that limit where they can take a better job.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Employer Collusion Act on July 23, 2019.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it was introduced 'for himself and Ms. Warren'.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: His committee, to which the bill was referred on July 23, 2019, took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of how the parties would have split; the only two senators on record supporting the bill were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired committee to which it was referred took no action.

industries.industry: Franchisors and franchise chains (fast food and similar)
industries.note: These companies are the bill's direct target: many franchise systems use agreements promising not to hire each other's employees, which limits workers' job options and holds down wages. The bill would force removal of those clauses and expose the companies to worker lawsuits.

Any employer party to a no-hire or no-poach arrangement — including through contractor-subcontractor agreements — would face FTC enforcement and private damages suits, and would lose a tool for retaining staff by restricting competitors' hiring.
The bill creates a new private right of action with attorney's fees and punitive damages, expanding the market for employment-related antitrust litigation on workers' behalf.
